🇲🇽🌱 <u>Mexico City Avoided a Million Tonnes of Emissions in One Year</u>

Opening Mexico City's Climate and Nature Action Week, Mayor Clara Brugada said her government avoided more than one million tonnes of greenhouse gases in the past year, twice Cabo Verde's annual emissions. Eco-technologies are now installed in 19,000 homes, with a target of 50,000, and recycling rose 45% in seven months. "There is no climate justice without social justice, nor social justice without gender justice," Brugada said. Her government is studying how to speed up the switch away from fossil fuels for power generation.

🇲🇽🏛️ <u>It's Now in the Constitution: Mexico's Leaders Must Hold Only One Nationality</u>

Mexico's Senate formally declared the single-nationality reform constitutional after 22 state legislatures ratified the changes to Articles 82, 116 and 122. Anyone running for president, governor or head of Mexico City's government must be Mexican by birth and hold no other citizenship. Once in office, they can't use a foreign passport, claim rights as a foreign citizen, or seek another country's diplomatic protection. "The Chamber of Senators declares the Decree approved," said Senate president Higinio Martínez. The decree now goes to the Chamber of Deputies, then to the DOF. PRI and PAN fought it to the end.

🇲🇽🏛️ <u>Mexico's Lower House Passes Sheinbaum's Law to Phase Out Cash</u>

Mexico's Chamber of Deputies approved the Digital Economy Law in general by 330 votes to 112. It is a presidential initiative sent on September 8 to move payments onto SPEI, CoDi, QR codes and cards. Toll booths and gas stations go first, and the digital CURP becomes valid ID for opening financial services. PAN, PRI and MC voted against, objecting to Hacienda's power to choose which sectors go cashless. Cash is where tax evasion and fuel theft hide, so it makes sense that the push starts at the gas pump.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>The US Cut Down "La Abuela" to Build Its Wall on the Sonora Border</u>

A cottonwood between 200 and 250 years old, older than the border itself, was felled Monday in Lochiel, Arizona, right on the line with Santa Cruz, Sonora, to make room for a double wall. Activists had camped beside it since July 29. Border Patrol agents surrounded the camp, kept them away while the machinery went in, and at least ten were detained, La Jornada reports. Three other historic cottonwoods in the same area had already been removed. The tree survived 1848 and the Gadsden Purchase. It didn't survive the wall.

🔥🇲🇽 "It would be worth it for the Bank of Mexico to do a review." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Oct 6, 2026 Contralínea listed lifetime Bank of Mexico pensions above the President's salary, which the Constitution sets as the cap for public servants: 150,000 pesos a month for ex-president Ernesto Zedillo, 330,000 for Guillermo Ortiz, 350,000 for Francisco Gil Díaz, 412,000 for Miguel Mancera Aguayo. The golden pensions reform caps payouts at CFE, Nafinsa, Banobras and other federal bodies, but the central bank was left out. Some of those officials worked only six years at the bank. Sheinbaum said this is not about workers' pensions, only those of governors and deputy governors, and Zedillo was neither.

🚨🇲🇽 "In Mexico, it is necessarily the people who must decide." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Oct 6, 2026 Contralínea asked about the network of Fernando Cerimedo, now on trial in Bolivia, and his partner Javier Negre. The outlet has linked it to the PRI leadership, Claudio X. González's Sí por México, and Dick Morris, who worked on the 2006 "danger to Mexico" campaign against López Obrador. Sheinbaum described how the network operates: their outlet La Derecha Diaria publishes mostly false news, they buy accounts with large followings, and they pay for AI-driven bots that feed the algorithms. Under Mexican law, an election can be annulled if foreign intervention that changed the result is proven.

🚨🇲🇽 "It can't be that one talks about the rule of law and then, when push comes to shove, doesn't meet the requirements." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Mañanera, Oct 6, 2026 Sheinbaum laid out the law on Querétaro's new international police academy, where the US ambassador laid the first stone. Article 117 of the Constitution bars states from making alliances or treaties with foreign powers. Any foreign security cooperation with a state needs approval from the federal high-level security group and the Foreign Ministry. Querétaro has nine such projects with US law enforcement agencies, approved since 2021. The academy is not one of them, even though Querétaro's security secretary said at the event that it is designed to receive training from US agencies. "Why? Because it is the law."
